blocks.text: Sea sparrow, that is, ostrich. Nor do more recent writers describe the ostrich's running to us otherwise. Leo Africanus, book 9: It has large black feathers in its wings, by which, though useless for flight, it is helped in running through frequent movement of the wings and tail. You may read the same in Marmol, Africa, book 1, chapter 23. So among the Arabs Alkazuinius: اذا عدت النعامة ارخت جناحيها الي رجليها فلا يسبقها شي من الحيوانات [idhā ʿadat al-naʿāma arkhat janāḥayhā ilā rijlayhā fa-lā yasbiquhā shayʾ min al-ḥayawānāt] When the ostrich runs, it lets its wings down as far as its feet, and no animal overtakes it. But in the same place a thing utterly false is related: اذا استقبلت الريح كان اشد ما اذا استدبرتها [idhā istaqbalat al-rīḥ kāna ashadd mā idhā istadbarathā] When it has the wind against it, it runs more vigorously than when it has it behind. This is contrary both to nature and to the testimonies of the ancients [II, 849]. So Abu Ubeid in the same place wears himself out in vain searching for the cause of this marvel. I cannot but add a proverb of the Arabs in Alcamus: ركب جناحي النعامة [rakiba janāḥay al-naʿāma] He rode the wings of the ostrich, that is, جد في الامر واجتهد [jadda fī al-amr wa-ijtahada] He did something with great zeal and diligence. Damir explains the same proverb at much greater length. But let it suffice to have shown from this that, in the opinion of the Arabs, nothing is swifter than the wings of ostriches. Exultation can also be attributed to the wings of ostriches in another sense. Cardano, book 10 De subtilitate: No bird has such charm or beauty in its feathers; for this reason soldiers adorn their helmets with no others. This was already the custom long ago. Theophrastus, Historia plantarum, book 4, chapter 5, on a certain Indian tree: Τὸ φύλλον τὴν μὲν μορφὴν πρόμηκες, τοῖς τῶν στρουθῶν πτεροῖς ὅμοιον, ἃ παρατίθενται παρὰ τὰ κράνη· [To phyllon tēn men morphēn promēkes, tois tōn strouthōn pterois homoion, ha paratithentai para ta kranē] The leaf, oblong in shape, like the plumes of ostriches which are put on helmets. Pliny, in the place cited above: And feathers adorning war crests and helmets. These feathers, moreover, are taken from the wings as well as from the tail. Nor is there any animal whose feathers are so even; accordingly we read that among the Egyptians the ostrich feather was the symbol of equity. Horus, book 2, near the end: Ἄνθρωπον ἴσως τὸ δίκαιον ἀπονέμοντα βουλόμενοι σημῆναι, στρουθοκαμήλου πτερὸν γράφουσι· τοῦτο γὰρ τὸ ζῶον πανταχόθεν ἴσα ἔχει τὰ πτερυγώματα παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων. [Anthrōpon isōs to dikaion aponemonta boulomenoi sēmēnai, strouthokamēlou pteron graphousi; touto gar to zōon pantachothen isa echei ta pterygōmata para tōn allōn.] Wishing to signify a man who distributes justice equally to all, they paint an ostrich feather: for this animal, beyond the rest, has the feathers of its wings equal on every side. This very thing adds grace and beauty to the wings of ostriches. 4. Besides the ostrich, the Sacred Writer describes ten animals in this and the following chapter, and the names of all of them are read, as a heading, right in the first hemistich. Thus he begins the description of the lion: Will you hunt the prey for the lioness? And when he passes from there to the raven: Who provided food for the raven? Then, coming to the ibexes, he says: Do you know when the ibexes of the rocks give birth? And afterwards of the wild ass: Who let the wild ass go free? And of the rim, which the interpreters take to be the unicorn: Will the rim be willing to serve you? Why then, by the same reasoning, should not the ostrich also be placed in the first part of the verse? Especially since the descriptions that follow, of the horse, the hawk, the eagle, and of Behemoth and Leviathan, always keep the same rule. Here, then, I shall believe the matter stands in the same way, and that in the first part of the verse is read the name of the animal whose vivid description follows, until someone produces a reason for a difference, and here none presents itself. 5. Since it is agreed that the following description pertains to the [col. 247] ostrich, its name had to be put first, just as with the ten other animals which are described by Job. But if רננים renanim are not ostriches, it is certain that the name of the ostrich appears nowhere in this verse. For it is certain that חסידה chasida, which they explain as ostrich, is not the ostrich; since it is a migratory bird, Ierem. VIII, 7, and flies aloft, [II, 850] Zachar. V, 9., and nests in fir trees, Ps. CIV, 17., and has its name from piety: חסידה chasida literally means pious. This name in no way suits the ostrich, since in Thren. IV, 3. and in this very passage the ostrich is described as a bird impious and pitiless towards its young. Unless they would have it called חסידה κατ᾽ ἀντίφρασιν [kat᾽ antiphrasin], in the way, namely, that they call the Furies Eumenides. Therefore the best interpreters, and even those very ones who would have chasida here be the ostrich, consistently render it elsewhere as stork. That this rendering is most true I shall prove at length in its place. Among the recent interpreters there is one learned and pious man to whom these things were by no means unknown. He, then, although carried away by the common error he takes רננים renanim for peacocks, nevertheless explains חסידה chasida as stork. But because the name of the ostrich could not be absent from this verse without sacrilege, he would have the last word נוצה be not only a bird, with R. Selomo, but the ostrich. But if נוצה is the name of a bird, since it is formed from flying (for the verb נצה means to fly), it will not fit the ostrich, which alone of birds lacks flight and never raises itself from the ground. What of the fact that נוצה is not even a bird? For נוצה signifies nothing other than feather or plumage. This is clear from Ezech. XVII, 3., where the eagle is described as מלא הנוצה, full of plumage, and רב נוצה, of much plumage, or abounding in plumage, as he himself renders it. Why then should a word which there means plumage be taken here for a bird, and indeed for the ostrich? Why should a new and unheard-of meaning be attached to this word, without witness, without example, without any shadow of reason, a meaning which the very origin of the word plainly refutes? From this it follows that the ostrich is not named in the last hemistich, and must therefore be sought in the first, namely in the word רננים renanim. Otherwise it would be entirely absent from this verse ^{(1)}. And when it is said in the verse immediately following, She leaves her eggs on the ground, etc. (which it is certain are said of the ostrich), these things would be said [II, 851] of a bird that has nowhere been named before, and the discourse would be left hanging, nor would these words cohere in any way with what precedes.
